schemaFit.detail: Against the documented Structured Outputs subset (guide read 2026-10-21). DOCUMENTED and fine: root object with all fields required and additionalProperties:false; enum of strings, including 16-hex ids that vary per call (limit 1,000 enum values per schema, 120,000 chars in total; the 15,000-char rule only binds a single enum above 250 values); anyOf for nullability written as anyOf:[{type:'null'}, ...] (shown in the guide's recursive example); nested anyOf (communication -> proximityUtterance -> referent), since 'nested schemas must each be valid per this subset'; minimum/maximum on price (unsupported only for fine-tuned models); nesting is assumed to stay under 10 levels (not measured). NOT DOCUMENTED: 'const', both string const on kind discriminators and numeric const on each move's x and y. The guide names const only in the 120,000-char limit. Strict mode errors on unsupported keywords, so a failure would be a 400 on the first call. Rewrite inside the documented subset: string const -> single-value string enum (enum:['wallPost']). Numeric const has two options: a single-value numeric enum, though no guide example shows numeric enum values, so that is also unverified; or, safest, replace the numeric {x,y} pins with one string enum of legal move ids. Either way the first live request is the test. A per-call schema also means no cross-call cache reuse and an unquantified first-request schema-processing latency on every call.

Same subset (the guide is model-independent; the GPT-6 guide says GPT-6 supports Structured Outputs). The same verdicts apply: const (string and numeric) is undocumented, so rewrite to single-value or string enums or test live; anyOf-null, nested anyOf and minimum/maximum are documented; per-call enums are fine within limits. Extra for this model: the default prompt_cache_options.mode 'implicit' writes the per-call prefix at 1.25x input. The schema precedes developer messages in the rendered prefix (guide illustration), so with a per-call schema no breakpoint yields reuse. Send prompt_cache_options:{mode:'explicit'} with no breakpoints. The current transport does not send prompt_cache_options, and the reference says that field is for gpt-5.6 and later only, so the transport needs a per-model setting.

Same as gpt-6-luna: const is undocumented, the other keywords are documented, and the implicit-cache default should be turned off with mode:'explicit'. Left in implicit mode, the worst-case request under the 32,768-byte body cap (at most 32,768 input tokens) with max_output_tokens 2048 books (32,768 x 0.25 + 2,048 x 1.2) x 2 = 21,299 micro-USD at the study's 2x rate. That exceeds the 20,000 micro-USD per-request ceiling. In explicit mode it is 18,022.

notes: Method: every OpenAI page was fetched on 2026-10-21 both as raw HTML (and, for pricing, the embedded component props) and as the official .md render (append .md). Prices were compared across the model page, the pricing .md table and the pricing HTML props. All three agree for every model listed.

Surprising claims, checked twice. (a) gpt-5.4-nano deprecation: confirmed by the deprecations page and by the model-page Deprecated badges; the changelog has no separate entry. (b) gpt-6-luna as a new, cheaper replacement: confirmed by the model page, the pricing page and the changelog (released 2026-09-22 at $0.10 / $0.01 / $0.50). (c) gpt-5-nano shutdown on 2026-12-11: confirmed by the deprecations page, the badge and the model page text.

DROPPED: gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14. All of its facts check out, but it shuts down on 2026-10-23, two days from now, before study 1 can be reactivated, so it cannot meet any requirement. The other five are kept. gpt-5-nano is kept only conditionally: it shuts down 2026-12-11, its effort values are undocumented, and it is unsuitable unless the study runs and finishes within about 7 weeks. gpt-4o-mini is kept with caveats: it shuts down 2027-01-14 and probably needs a transport change to omit the reasoning parameter.

REFUTED: the claim that first-request schema-processing latency affects only fine-tuned models. The Structured Outputs guide says 'the first request you make with any schema will have additional latency'. Our schema is rebuilt for every actor and tick, so every call can pay this unquantified cost. With no published latency figure, the 16 s per-call budget is unverified on every candidate, Standard tier included, and must be measured on the first live calls.

CORRECTED: where the schema sits in the cache prefix. The caching guide's illustration places 'tools and schemas' before the developer-message prefix. With a per-call schema, a breakpoint after the rules text cannot produce reuse. The researcher's alternative fix, a breakpoint after at least 1,024 stable tokens, does not work unless the schema is made byte-identical across calls. For gpt-6-luna and gpt-5.6-luna, use prompt_cache_options.mode:'explicit' with no breakpoints, which means no caching and no write charge.

CORRECTED: the 12h caching conflict. The changelog of 2026-10-20 announces that 12h caching is available (writes at 2.5x). The API reference is inconsistent with itself: request-level ttl lists only '30m', while per-breakpoint ttl allows '30m' or '12h'. This does not matter for this workload because nothing is reusable.

NEW, not in the claims: on 2026-10-21 (today) the changelog reports that projects can now restrict which service tiers they may use. The transport sends service_tier:'default', which the API reference still lists as valid, so check the project's tier settings before the first live call. The earlier live attempt returned HTTP 401, an authentication failure, not a schema result.

NEW, not in the claims: the Decisions API (beta since 2026-10-06; gpt-6-luna only; POST /v1/decisions) returns typed answers 'about 10x faster than the Responses API'. Its outputs are only predicate, choice or score. The guide says to use Structured Outputs for your own JSON schema. It cannot express our nested move/communication/diary/role object, so it is not a fit without redesigning the decision format.

Hard-requirement status. (1) Strict schema: every candidate supports Structured Outputs, but 'const' (string and numeric) is undocumented everywhere; acceptance is unverified for ALL models, including the current one, until a first real request; the fix is single-value or string enums. (2) Low reasoning: documented for gpt-5.4-nano, gpt-6-luna and gpt-5.6-luna; unverified for gpt-5-nano; not applicable to gpt-4o-mini. (3) Temperature: not required. (4) Synchronous within about 16 s: Standard tier is synchronous but has no published latency; Flex has no SLA and 'more likely' timeouts; Batch (24h window only) needs one batch per tick, 6 sequential rounds for study 1.

Cost ranking at 9k in / 300 out, Standard list price, no cache, before reasoning tokens (recomputed): gpt-5-nano $0.000570 < gpt-6-luna $0.001050 < gpt-4o-mini $0.001530 < gpt-5.6-luna $0.002160 = about gpt-5.4-nano $0.002175. Booked at 2x for 630 calls: $0.72 / $1.32 / $1.93 / $2.72 / $2.74, all within the USD 5 allowance. Worst case under the 32,768-byte body and 2,048 output cap, booked at 2x: gpt-5.4-nano 18,227 micro-USD, which fits the 20,000 ceiling; gpt-5.6-luna in implicit mode 21,299, which exceeds it.

Reproducibility: gpt-6-luna and gpt-5.6-luna publish no dated snapshot; the API reference's model enum also lists only the aliases. Moving study 1 off its pinned gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17 changes its manifest, allowance and contract. That decision belongs to the owner. gpt-5.4-nano itself stays available until 2027-04-01.
Not covered here: other providers and the local RTX 4070 Ti Super option. This pass verified only the OpenAI claims supplied.

models.cheaperTiers: Standard prices: $0.25 input / $1.50 output / $0.025 cached for text, image and video (audio costs more). Cache storage is $1.00 per 1M tokens per hour. Batch: $0.125 / $0.75 / $0.0125, cache storage $0.50. Batch is asynchronous with a 24-hour target turnaround and runs through generateContent only (not the Interactions API). Flex has the same prices as Batch; it is synchronous but in PREVIEW, with a 1-15 minute latency target and best-effort, sheddable capacity (503s possible, no fallback to Standard), so it cannot meet ~16 s. Priority: $0.45 / $2.70 / $0.045, cache storage $1.80. Priority is in PREVIEW and its latency is listed as 'Seconds'. Traffic over the Priority limit (0.3x the Standard limit) is silently downgraded to Standard and billed at Standard rates, so Priority does not guarantee latency. Standard latency is listed only as 'Seconds to minutes'.
models.deprecation: GA/Stable, released 2026-05-07 (confirmed on the deprecations page and in the release notes). Earliest possible shutdown is 2027-05-07 and the recommended replacement is gemini-3.5-flash-lite. The shutdown date appears only on the deprecations page; I found no release-notes announcement for it. Google says it will give advance notice of the exact date.
models.reasoningControl: thinking_level (generateContent: generationConfig.thinkingConfig.thinkingLevel; Interactions API: thinking_level), with levels minimal/low/medium/high. The API reference describes MINIMAL as 'Little to no thinking'. The Gemini 3 guide says minimal 'does not guarantee that thinking is off', and the OpenAI-compat page says reasoning cannot be turned off for Gemini 3 models. The DEFAULT is contradictory across official pages: the Gemini 3 guide's table marks minimal 'Supported (Default)' for 3.1 Flash-Lite, but the same page says 'If thinking_level is not specified, Gemini 3 will default to high', and the thinking page's default table omits this model. Set the level explicitly. Thinking tokens are billed at the output price.
models.strictJsonSchema: Partial; needs a rewrite and a live test. The current generateContent field is generationConfig.responseFormat.text.schema with mimeType APPLICATION_JSON. responseSchema (legacy OpenAPI Schema, which has no additionalProperties and string-only enum) and _responseJsonSchema are marked deprecated. The Interactions API takes response_format {type:'text', mime_type:'application/json', schema}, and that is the only form the structured-output guide documents. The guide lists: type (including 'null', with nullability written as a type array); title; description; properties; required; additionalProperties; enum for strings and numbers; format; minimum/maximum; items; prefixItems; minItems/maxItems (enforced). anyOf and $ref appear in its examples. The wider list ($id/$defs/$ref/$anchor, oneOf treated as anyOf, propertyOrdering) comes only from the DEPRECATED _responseJsonSchema description in the API reference. `const` is not documented anywhere. minLength/maxLength/minProperties/maxProperties/uniqueItems/contains/minContains/maxContains are stripped silently. A schema can be rejected with 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT ('too many states or too much branching'). The documented causes include very long property or enum names, enums with many values, anyOf with many alternatives, long runs of optional properties, large maxItems, AND numeric minimum/maximum bounds. Google promises only 'syntactically correct JSON' and says to validate values.

schemaFit.detail: (1) Numeric const {type:'number', const:3} is undocumented: rewrite it as {type:'number', enum:[3]}, since numeric enum is documented. (2) String const {type:'string', const:'wallPost'}: rewrite it as {type:'string', enum:['wallPost']}. (3) anyOf:[{type:'null'}, ...]: 'null' is a documented type, but the only documented nullable form is a type array ({type:['string','null']}). A standalone {type:'null'} branch is undocumented and must be tested. A multi-alternative union such as move (up to ~5 objects) cannot be turned into a type array, so if the null branch is refused there is no clean rewrite short of an explicit 'none' variant. (4) Nested anyOf (communication -> proximityUtterance -> referent): anyOf is shown in examples, but nesting depth is undocumented, and 'anyOf with many alternatives' is a listed cause of 400s. (5) minimum/maximum on price is documented as supported, but 'numeric minimum/maximum bounds' is ALSO a listed cause of the 400 complexity error. If the request is rejected, drop the bounds and keep client-side validation. (6) additionalProperties:false and required are documented in the JSON-schema path. Do NOT send through legacy responseSchema, which has no additionalProperties and only string enums. (7) Per-call enums of 16-hex/64-hex ids are supported in principle, but 'very long ... enum names' and 'enums with many values' are listed causes of 400. The schema changes every call, and no compiled-grammar cache is documented. (8) Output is promised only as 'syntactically correct JSON', so keep the existing post-validation. All of this needs one live request with the largest real schema.

Same documented subset and limits as gemini-3.1-flash-lite: numeric const becomes a one-value numeric enum, and string const becomes a one-value string enum. A standalone {type:'null'} anyOf branch is undocumented and must be tested. Nested anyOf and wide anyOf carry complexity-400 risk, and so do the minimum/maximum bounds on price. additionalProperties:false is supported only on the JSON-schema path (responseFormat.text.schema, or the Interactions response_format.schema). Long or many 16-hex/64-hex enum values are a listed rejection cause. Keep post-validation. The model page says 'Structured outputs: Supported'.

Same rewrites as the Gemini 3 Flash-Lite models: const becomes a one-value enum; the standalone {type:'null'} anyOf branch must be tested; the nested and wide anyOf, the min/max bounds and the long or many enum values carry complexity-400 risk. Extra uncertainty: the docs do not say per model that 2.5 accepts the same JSON-schema keyword subset through responseFormat.text.schema. The legacy responseSchema path cannot express additionalProperties:false or numeric enums. Access to 2.5 models may be refused to a new project, which would make the fit question moot.

Same documented subset and limits as the other Gemini models. Rewrite numeric and string const as one-value enums. Test the standalone {type:'null'} anyOf branch, the nested anyOf, the min/max bounds and the 16-hex/64-hex enum lists against the complexity limit. Keep post-validation. Google's own anyOf, enum and recursive $ref examples target this model on the Interactions API, but that is evidence about the keywords, not about our schema's size.

notes: METHOD: Every cited page was downloaded as raw HTML from ai.google.dev on 2026-10-21 and converted to text locally; no summariser was used. I also read four pages the claims did not cite: priority-inference, interactions, gemini-3 and changelog. Every page's 'Last updated' stamp matches the dates the claims give. Every price, release date, shutdown date, context size, thinking level, rate-limit figure and caching figure in the claims matches the official pages. None was refuted.

CORRECTIONS THAT MATTER: (a) The broad keyword list ($ref/$defs/$id/$anchor, oneOf, propertyOrdering) comes from the DEPRECATED `_responseJsonSchema` field description. The current structured-output guide documents a narrower list, and only for the Interactions API's response_format.schema. (b) 'numeric minimum/maximum bounds' is also a documented cause of the 400 complexity rejection, and our schema uses min/max on price. (c) The default thinking for 3.1 Flash-Lite is contradictory across official pages (minimal versus high), so set it explicitly. (d) Flex and Priority are both Preview, and Priority silently downgrades overflow to Standard. (e) The Interactions API is GA and recommended for new projects, generateContent is 'legacy', and the Interactions API stores requests unless store=false. (f) 2.5 Flash-Lite thinking control conflicts between the thinking page and the API reference.

DROPPED: none. On documented evidence no model fails a hard requirement. Strict structured output is achievable with the const-to-enum rewrites, pending a live test. Low or minimal reasoning is available on all four (3.8 Flash has low but not minimal). Synchronous ~16 s is unverified for every model, because Google gives no latency figure beyond Standard 'Seconds to minutes'. Flex (1-15 min) and Batch (24 h) are unusable for the per-tick loop; Batch could work only if a whole tick across episodes were batched and waited on.

FLAG, gemini-3.8-flash against Study 1 accounting (my arithmetic on confirmed prices, at the project's 2x booking): typical calls (5-9k input, 100-300 output, no thinking) come to 714 x 2 x $0.0041-0.0079, or about $5.9-11.2. That exceeds the USD 5 allowance before any thinking tokens. Worst case per request (9k input + 2,048 output) is about 28,860 micro-USD, above the 20,000 per-request ceiling, and about 57,700 after the 2027-01-01 price doubling. The other three fit the per-request ceiling at Standard: 2.5 FL ~3,440, 3.1 FL ~10,640, 3.5 FL ~15,640 micro-USD worst case. 3.5 FL at Priority (~28,150) would not. Study 1 is pinned to gpt-5.4-nano in any case, so any switch needs a new manifest, allowance and contract.

FLAG, gemini-2.5-flash-lite is the cheapest on paper ($0.10/$0.40), but Google states that access to 2.5 models is limited to users who have actively used them in the past. A new or unused project may be refused. Verify with one call before planning around it.

TRANSPORT: there is no OpenAI Responses API endpoint. The options are (1) OpenAI Chat Completions compat at /v1beta/openai/ (beta; strict json_schema behaviour undocumented); (2) the Interactions API (/v1beta/interactions: model, input, response_format{type:'text', mime_type:'application/json', schema}, service_tier, store=false), which is GA, recommended, and close in shape to the Responses API but not wire-compatible; (3) generateContent with generationConfig.responseFormat.text.schema, which is required for Batch and explicit caching. A new adapter is needed in every case. Keep the existing 32 KB fail-closed body limit and the post-validation.

FIRST-REQUEST TEST PLAN: send the actual largest per-call schema, after rewriting const as one-value enums, to each candidate at the chosen thinking level. Record whether the response is a 400 complexity rejection, whether a standalone {type:'null'} branch inside anyOf is accepted, the usage metadata (input, thinking and output tokens, cached tokens) and the wall-clock latency. Also check whether an un-rewritten numeric const is rejected or silently dropped. Silently dropping it would leave move x/y unconstrained, so never rely on it.

OTHER: (a) Temperature, top_p and top_k are deprecated and silently ignored on Gemini 3.6 Flash and newer (API reference; changelog 2026-07-21). That is harmless here because determinism is not required. (b) Gemma 4 models (gemma-4-31b-it, gemma-4-26b-a4b-it) are listed on the Interactions API, but the pricing page shows the paid tier as 'Not available', and on the free tier content is 'Used to improve our products: Yes'. So they are not a hosted candidate for this study, and their local use is outside this verification. (c) Token counts were estimated with OpenAI's tokenizer; Gemini's will differ, so every cost figure above is an estimate until usage metadata from a real call is in hand.
